summary:
Limpopo is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national legal framework. The province-specific material in the source inventory concerns the reach of customary law and traditional authority in the rural districts that formed part of the former Bantustans.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people living in the former Bantustans, with no provision allowing anyone to opt out of its jurisdiction. The same account reports that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas.

Mamba Online published a account by Melanie Judge on 18 April 2012 stating that the Traditional Courts Bill, then under debate in provincial public hearings, would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system. Lesbians are reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices with no opt-out from that jurisdiction, and those with the means are expected to leave rural areas as a result. The same account records that traditional leaders also opposed the 2006 Civil Union Act.

The most recent documented instance in this record is from 2012; no later instance is documented.
tangentialFactors:
The documented exposure in Limpopo is institutional rather than incidental: the punishments described are administered at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, and the jurisdiction is compulsory for people resident in the former-Bantustan districts. The reported response of those able to do so is relocation from rural areas to cities, which places the burden of avoidance on the person targeted rather than on the authority imposing the punishment.

Traditional leaders' opposition to the 2006 Civil Union Act, recorded in April 2012, indicates that hostility in this layer of authority extends to relationship recognition as well as to conduct. Poor police cooperation reported for rural LGBT residents in May 2012 compounds the problem, since the ordinary protection machinery and the customary system are documented as failing at the same time.
localsOnly:
Residents of Limpopo's former-Bantustan rural districts fall under the jurisdiction of chiefs' courts under the customary system described by Human Rights Watch on 29 May 2012, with no opt-out available to anyone within that jurisdiction.

Rural LGBT residents are reported to face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and lesbians are reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, per Human Rights Watch (29 May 2012) and Mamba Online (18 April 2012). Traditional leaders in the province are recorded as having opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the Traditional Courts Bill is unresolved in this record: both sources describe it as before parliament or under provincial debate in 2012, and no source states whether it was subsequently enacted, amended or withdrawn.

No documentation after 2012 is available for this province, so the present operation of customary jurisdiction over LGBT residents, the current state of police cooperation in rural districts, and any enforcement of the national hate-crime regime through traditional courts are all not sourced here.

This record contains no Limpopo-specific material on identity-document rules, legal gender recognition, access to gender-affirming care, facility access, or documented incidents of violence against trans people in the province.
